title: Classes and objects
summary: A class is a blueprint: typed properties, constructors, and constants in one object.

blocks.html:
A class is a blueprint. It lists the data one thing holds, and the names that data goes by. An object is one thing built from that blueprint, carrying its own copy of every property.

This chapter and the two after it build up to src/GradeCalculator.php, the class that powers the grade calculator page. We start much smaller.

blocks.title: score.php
blocks.code:
<?php

class Score
{
    public string $label;
    public float $value;
}

$quiz = new Score();
$quiz->label = 'Quiz';
$quiz->value = 88.5;

echo $quiz->label, ': ', $quiz->value, "\n";

$final = new Score();
$final->label = 'Final';
$final->value = 92.0;

echo $final->label, ': ', $final->value, "\n";
echo $quiz->label, ' is still ', $quiz->value, "\n";

blocks.title: one blueprint, two objects
blocks.ascii:
class Score (the blueprint)
    label: string
    value: float

  new Score()          new Score()
  ------------         ------------
  label = 'Quiz'       label = 'Final'
  value = 88.5         value = 92.0

  Two objects, two independent sets of values.

blocks.html:
public string $label; declares a property with a type. PHP checks every write against it: in the default coercive mode a compatible value such as 42 is converted to "42", and in strict mode a mismatch is a TypeError.

Because the type is declared, PHP also refuses to read the property before anything is assigned: an uninitialized typed property throws an Error, instead of quietly handing you null.

new Score() builds the object and -> reaches inside it. Writing creates nothing: it fills a slot that already exists.

Assigning a property the class never declared used to silently invent it. Since PHP 8.2 that is deprecated: $quiz->bonus = 5; raises a deprecation notice. #[AllowDynamicProperties] exists only to keep old code quiet, and you do not need it here. Declare the property.

blocks.title: a constructor does the setting up
blocks.code:
<?php

class Score
{
    public string $label;
    public float $value;

    public function __construct(string $label, float $value)
    {
        $this->label = $label;
        $this->value = $value;
    }
}

$quiz = new Score('Quiz', 88.5);
$final = new Score('Final', 92.0);

echo $quiz->label, ': ', $quiz->value, "\n";
echo $final->label, ': ', $final->value, "\n";

blocks.html:
__construct() runs once, when new runs, with whatever you pass in the parentheses. Its job is to leave every property set, so no object is ever half-built.

PHP 8 shortens that ceremony. Put a visibility keyword on the constructor parameter and it becomes a property, assigned for you. Add readonly and the property can be written once, from inside the class, and never again.

blocks.title: constructor property promotion
blocks.code:
<?php

class Score
{
    public function __construct(
        public readonly string $label,
        public readonly float $value,
    ) {}
}

$quiz = new Score('Quiz', 88.5);

echo $quiz->label, ': ', $quiz->value, "\n";

// $quiz->value = 90.0;
// Error: Cannot modify readonly property Score::$value

blocks.html:
Some values belong to the class rather than to any one object: the four weights never differ between calculators. Those are class constants, declared with const and read with ::. No object is needed, and :: is also how you call a method that does not need one.

The real calculator keeps its weights as private const WEIGHTS. A private member can only be read from inside the class body: the outside world asks getWeightedScores() instead, and never learns how the numbers are stored. That is the whole point, and the next chapter owns the detail.

blocks.title: :: for the class, -> for the object
blocks.code:
<?php

class Score
{
    public const MAX = 100;

    public function __construct(
        public readonly string $label,
        public readonly float $value,
    ) {}
}

echo 'top of the scale: ', Score::MAX, "\n";
echo 'the label of one object: ', (new Score('Quiz', 88.5))->label, "\n";
blocks.output:
top of the scale: 100
the label of one object: Quiz

blocks.title: src/GradeCalculator.php, the top of the class
blocks.code:
<?php

class GradeCalculator
{
    private const WEIGHTS = [
        'quiz' => 0.20,
        'assignment' => 0.20,
        'midterm' => 0.25,
        'final' => 0.35,
    ];

    public function __construct(
        private readonly float $quiz,
        private readonly float $assignment,
        private readonly float $midterm,
        private readonly float $final,
    ) {}
}

quiz.q: What does new Score() hand back?
options: A copy of the class source
One object with its own properties
quiz.why: The class is the blueprint; new builds one object from it. Two objects from the same class hold separate values.

quiz.q: A property is declared as promoted and readonly. Which statement is true?
options: It can be written many times from anywhere
It is written once, from inside the class, and never again
It is shared by every object of the class
quiz.why: The visibility keyword on the parameter makes it a property, and readonly allows exactly one write, which the promoted constructor performs. Values shared by all objects are class constants.

quiz.q: You write $score->bonus = 5 but Score declares no $bonus. What does PHP 8.4 do?
quiz.why: Dynamic properties were deprecated in PHP 8.2. The property is still created, but the notice tells you to declare it, which is what #[AllowDynamicProperties] only papers over.

exercise.brief: Write a class Course with a promoted readonly string $name and int $credits, plus a public constant PASSING set to 75. Build the course PHP with 3 credits and print one line: PHP/3/75.
exercise.starter:
<?php

// class Course, then one object, then one line
exercise.hint: Promotion keeps the whole constructor in the signature: public function __construct(public readonly string $name, public readonly int $credits) {}. A constant is read through the class: Course::PASSING.
exercise.solution:
<?php

class Course
{
    public const PASSING = 75;

    public function __construct(
        public readonly string $name,
        public readonly int $credits,
    ) {}
}

$course = new Course('PHP', 3);

echo $course->name, '/', $course->credits, '/', Course::PASSING, "\n";
